text.p: In recent years, it has been difficult to find a decent fund that invests in overseas markets. At least, that's what you would think if you relied on the popular "star" rating system used by Morningstar Inc. the Chicago-based mutual fund research firm.
In truth, however, there are plenty of decent international stock funds -- and a major change in the Morningstar system will now make it easier to find them.
The old system compared the performance of international funds to a group that included both those funds and funds that invest primarily in U.S. stocks.

During recent years, U.S. stocks have outgained overseas stock markets by a wide margin. Foreign funds have a five-year annualized return of 10.5 percent compared to 16.1 percent for domestic equity funds.
As a result, even the best international funds haven't been able to keep up with their domestic peers.

Indeed, as of October, out of the 95 international funds, not one rated five stars (highest). Two rated four stars (above average) and 10 rated three stars (neutral). Another 22 rated two stars (below average) and 61 rated one star (lowest).
In other words, 83 of the 95 international funds rated below average or worse.

By contrast, only 209 of the 1,262 domestic funds rated below average or worse. Even the most respected international funds around, such as T. Rowe Price International and Scudder International, were squeezed into the two-star category.
That situation was unfair to the funds. Worse, it made it difficult for investors who wanted to invest in a well-managed overseas fund as a diversification measure.
Investors who wanted to put some money to work overseas on the chance that those markets would rebound had to work harder to identify the best funds to do the job.

The new rating system recognises those problems. Henceforth, ratings for international funds will be based on the funds' performances relative to other international funds. If a fund has outperformed its peers on the international scene, the fund will receive a high star rating.
For example, since the new system began, 16 international funds have received a four-star rating or better.
What's more, the number of one-star international funds has decreased to 36.

The new system isn't perfect. For example, funds that invest in particular regions of the world will still be compared to those that invest in many different regions. Thus, it's important to use the star rating as a starting point only, and compare funds' gains and losses to those of other funds that invest in similar regions or market sectors abroad.

Still, the new star system will make it easier for investors to identify solid international funds. Among those funds: EuroPacific Growth (800-421-4120; $250 minimum investment; 5.75 percent load), which typically invests most of its assets in shares of large companies in Europe and the Pacific Rim. The fund's four-star rating remains the same under the new system.

Putnam International Growth (800-225-1581; $500 minimum; 5.75 percent load) takes a value-oriented approach to international investing. Manager Justin Scott recently invested a significant stake in shares of large companies in Japan and the Netherlands. Previously, the fund rated only two stars; under the new system it gets a four-star rating.

Finally, Morningstar's rating for the USAA International Fund (800-382-8722; $3,000 minimum; no-load) has increased from three stars to four. The fund turned in top-quintile returns during recent three- and five-year periods. The fund also carries a below-average expense ratio compared to other international funds. Manager David Peebles recently favoured holdings in Europe and emerging markets such as Hong Kong.
